vignette:
Mikaele, a 45-year-old chef whose hands once moved with the precision and passion of an artist, now felt like a stranger in his own kitchen. His divorce was final, his once-vibrant life feeling hollowed out, a direct consequence, he believed, of the night that had irrevocably altered him. He had been walking home after a late shift, still buzzing from the satisfaction of a busy service, when he was attacked and raped in a dimly lit alley. The assault itself was a blur of terror and pain, but its aftermath had calcified into a relentless mental burden.

In the months that followed, Mikaele found himself in a strange paradox regarding the event. He could talk about what happened very easily, recounting the bare facts of the assault to his therapist or even, in the early days, to his now ex-wife. Yet, despite this verbal access, he found that he could not put the memories of the event in the right order. Details were jumbled, timelines confused, like a recipe with missing or misplaced steps. More distressingly, he often found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, a sudden mental block descending when a specific image or sensation threatened to surface completely.

This fragmented, elusive memory was deeply intertwined with a pervasive sense of self-condemnation that had taken root within him. He felt dirty or contaminated because of what happened, a visceral revulsion that made him scrub his hands raw after preparing food, despite the meticulous hygiene his profession demanded. This feeling of being tainted extended beyond his body, seeping into his very identity. He was certain that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him - the spontaneous creativity, the confident command of a bustling kitchen, the intuitive understanding of flavors. His knife skills, once celebrated, now felt clumsy, his palate dulled. What was the point, he often wondered, when he felt so fundamentally broken? This deeply ingrained belief that his life has been destroyed by the trauma acted like a filter, ensuring that any attempt to fully process the event would be met with overwhelming despair. The sheer weight of this conviction, that his identity was shattered and his future irrevocably bleak, made it unbearable to confront the full, unvarnished memory. It was as if his mind, in a desperate act of self-preservation, would rather keep the details jumbled and incomplete than allow the full horror to confirm his darkest appraisals about himself.

His once-thriving career as a head chef at a popular restaurant in Honolulu had suffered immensely. The constant pressure, the necessity of close physical proximity with his team, the demand for precision and passion-all became agonizing reminders of his perceived contamination and lost capability. He began to delegate more, to withdraw from the creative process, eventually leading to his demotion and, ultimately, his resignation. He now works alone, catering small, private events, a stark contrast to the vibrant kitchens he once commanded. The smell of certain spices, the clatter of pots, even the sound of his own heavy breathing during a rush, could sometimes bring a sudden, overwhelming sense of dread, though he couldn't always pinpoint why.

Mikaele's PCL-5 score of 70 reflected the profound disruption to his life. He finally sought help, driven by a quiet desperation to reclaim some semblance of his former self. He still harboured the crushing certainty that his life was irrevocably ruined, but a tiny flicker of hope remained-a faint desire to understand why his mind refused to let him remember clearly, and whether the man he once was could ever truly be recovered from the wreckage.
